title: Leaving Chicago for Detroit and stopping recording
summary: She moved to Detroit in 1929 at her husband's brother's urging, hated recording, and the companies lost track of her; she played cabarets with a five-piece band.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Well, let me ask you something, Ms. Wallace. Now, in 1929 you stopped singing for recordings, right?
Yeah (inaudible).
For a while.
(Inaudible).
They didn't know where you were?
Yeah.
Where were you?
Detroit.
Oh, I see. You left Chicago and you went to Detroit?
My husband's brother told me to come to Detroit. And --
That's your second husband?
Yeah -- no, that was my real husband.
That's your first husband?
Yeah.
I see. So you went to Detroit in 1929? Is that it.
To live.
Yeah. And they didn't know where you were, the O.K. people.

Uh-huh. Because see, they -- I wanted to -- I wanted (unintelligible). But Mr. Pierce was supposed to be my manager, I thought he would let me (unintelligible). See, I didn't know he didn't have music with the O.K. people. He must have held me because they -- he left them up there. Somebody must have helped him.
Well, didn't you care? Didn't you care that you weren't recording any more?
No, no, I hated it.
You didn't care?

No, I hated. I hated working recording. And my said they had asked him if he he had been asked to tell my brother -- tell Sipple something. But they were stopped communicating about me, they was communicating to me. But they communicated with my brother, George, I wouldn't have been (unintelligible).
But now, Ms. Wallace, when you moved to Detroit, you left Chicago and moved to Detroit, did you know that you were going to be giving up your recording?

No, I thought my brother would -- I thought they would contact my brother and my brother would tell me like he did before, you know. But my brother said they didn't tell him. So finally they told Brother, they said, well, George, if we can't find Sippie, it's been over a year -- I think he said it'd been ten years or something, he said, (unintelligible). He said, well, I'll get in touch with her. See.
What were you doing in Detroit? Just living?
I played for cabarets.
Played for cabarets.

I had a band. I had a five piece orchestra. And I played for ______ parties, usually we'd play, some give them on Mondays, some give them Tuesday nights, some give them Wednesday nights (inaudible) somebody's going to give another party.
So you earned money playing for parties?
Oh, yeah, oh, yeah, I was regular.
So you were working all the time?
Oh, yes, I was working all the time (inaudible) party.
